word_order: SVO | Most sample clauses show Subject–Verb–Object order (e.g. 'The game is based...', 'Blood goes away from the heart...'), with postposed modifiers and many relative/subordinate clauses.
register: Written expository / encyclopedic/news style (formal, edited prose like encyclopedia or newswire rather than spontaneous speech).
non_boundary_traps: comma-separated lists (e.g. 'Korean, Thai, Indian, and Japanese')
notes_for_prompt_writer: Do not emit a translation unit immediately after a head noun if the next token is one of the unstable_prefix_signals above — English relative pronouns, 'called'/appositive markers and prepositions commonly add modifiers that Japanese must place before the noun. Commas are unreliable boundaries: they frequently introduce appositives or lists rather than sentence-final breaks. Prefer splitting at clear clause-connectors like coordinating conjunctions that start independent clauses, and only split after nouns when no relative/subordinate marker or preposition follows.

target_language_profile.word_order: Basic SOV: modifiers and relative clauses precede heads; topic-fronting common (は). Verb-finality is rigid; topical/adverbial ordering has some freedom (see 1,9,11,12).
target_language_profile.verb_placement: Main verb and predicate land clause-final, so tense/aspect/modality/negation and clause closure must be deferred until the verb appears (see 2,6,15).
late_commitment_forced_by: relative-clause attachment and prenominal modifier placement (see 2,9,11)
case/particle choice and topic vs subject marking (は/が/を) (see 1,12,13)
target_language_profile.reordering_vs_source: Large reordering: verbs move to sentence end; English postnominal modifiers become prenominal; topics/adverbials often fronted. Noun-modifier order flips relative to English (see 1,9,11).
safe_boundary_signals: sentence-final punctuation (period, question mark) — clause can be rendered (see 2,6)
explicit finite/main verb that closes the clause in source (see 6,15)
unsafe_boundary_signals: noun immediately followed by relative pronoun ('which/who/that') or comma + clause (see 2,9)
subordinating words like 'pending','when','as','because' that attach later (see 8,11)
comma/semicolon lists where attachment of items is unresolved (see 15)
